speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to express my appreciation for the kind remarks by the Hon. Member for Levis (Mr. Fontaine). Obviously the Hon. Member is a very intelligent, hard-working, industrious Member of Parliament and represents his constituents well. Indeed, he carries a very strong and continuing interest in the welfare of the agricultural community, not only in his province but in the country as a whole. He regularly attends rural caucus meetings and communicates problems on behalf of his constituents to me on a frequent and regular basis. It is a pleasure to be associated with him.
The Hon. Member has utilized what little time is available to him tonight to point to some of the major initiatives and programs we brought forward for the benefit not only of Quebec agriculture, but of Canadian agriculture. I am sure that he, if time permitted, would have made the observation that since we assumed office, we have taken somewhere in the vicinity of 235 initiatives, directing well over $5 billion to our agricultural industry. At the same time we should take note of the Prime Minister's observation as of April 30, when we delivered the last farm finance package, that indeed more had to be done.
Coming specifically to the question the Hon. Member raised, let me tell him that in March of this year I wrote to my colleague, the Minister of Agriculture of the Province of Quebec, requesting that he, on behalf of his Government, make a decision with respect to signing an agricultural subagreement. We had made representations on this subject to the previous Government. However, they could not make up their minds as to whether they wanted to sign an agreement both in agriculture and fisheries or on how to divide the federal allocation.
With the election of a new Government, the new Minister responded to my letter on April 23, I believe, indicating they had taken the decision and he was prepared to enter into an agricultural sub-agreement to the extent of some $36 million. Most of that money will be spent in research and development, and again we are happy to sign an agreement of that kind because of the priority we place on research and development.
I have replied to the Minister, indicating that we should instruct the appropriate officials in both our Departments to get together and work out the details. It is my understanding, from information I received earlier today, that the meeting will indeed take place next week.
May 29, 1986

Mr. Speaker, the question I wish to address this evening is one I raised with the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) during Question Period on May 2. It has to do with authorizing a revolutionary waste disposal unit for use in Canada. There are a number of industrial waste dump sites, particularly in southern Ontario, which allow the seepage of harmful chemicals into waterways like the Niagara River and, from there, into our drinking water. It is a source of concern to all who live in the densely populated regions of southern Ontario. As you and I both know, the federal Government is very concerned about this matter.
Recently the Environment Minister and the Minister responsible for emergency planning announced steps to respond to major chemical accidents in Canada. This is an important and timely development. My concern, however, is with the every-day dumping of chemical waste products from Canadian and American sources. We know that putting it into containers will not help. Over time containers deteriorate and we are right back where we started.
As I mentioned earlier in this House, the E. S. Fox Company, located in my riding of Welland, has developed a mobile waste disposal unit called the pyroplasma, which has been proven effective in the destruction of PCBs. This unit is unique. Its competition is essentially incinerators which have approximately a 99.99 per cent destruction efficiency rate. The pyroplasma unit has an unofficial destruction efficiency rate of 99.9999999 per cent. This is a consistent percentage when one is talking of a million pounds of waste material. Those extra nines make a lot of difference.
The provincial and federal Governments have actively participated in developing test procedures which will set permit application guidelines for waste disposal units. The commitment is there, but it is taking a long time.
The Province of Ontario has asked for proposals to clean up the Smithville site. These are to be submitted within the next few days. The local public know what the pyroplasma can do and want it to be used. They know what those extra nines mean. Other Canadians living close to industrial dumping sites are crying out for this kind of efficient answer to the problem.
The federal and provincial Governments have already invested half a million dollars into this project. The United States awarded the E. S. Fox Company a $2 million demonstration contract to finance the actual building of the unit, which could then be used to clean up the Love Canal area in New York State. Earlier this month the pyroplasma was set up at that site.
After four or five months of test procedures on dioxin and more than 100 other chemicals located there, it will be put into full use in clean-up operations.
Adjournment Debate
Over the past 10 years 17,000 gallons of waste products have been pumped out of the ground and stored at the Love Canal site. When the pyroplasma is put into full operation, it will take only 30 days to destroy that material. The company will go back once a year to destroy the waste which has been pumped out over that year.
We can all be very proud of the fact that this technology has been developed entirely in Canada. Despite considerable investment of American funds, it is still wholly owned by a Canadian company, a company which is continually looking at new ways to combat environmental problems.
At present the pyroplasma is being used to destroy liquid industrial waste. The same technology can be used on solid waste products. It is merely a matter of developing different material handling technology. There have been offers to fund the research necessary to develop such technology, provided free access to the technology is given in return. The company does not want to relinquish control to only one interested party. Too much has been invested. The pyroplasma has been extensively tested in Kingston under the supervision and with the financial backing of both federal and provincial Governments. The unit is completely mobile and can be set up in just a few days. What this will mean in future emergency clean-up situations is incredible.
The American Environmental Protection Agency ranks the pyroplasma in the top five technologies for waste disposal in the world. The word in the hallways at the EPA meeting last month was that this was the "-hottest piece of chemistry to come down the road in years".
My question was specifically when we could start putting this amazing technology to work in Canada. The question is a difficult one given the divided jurisdiction in the matter, but I firmly believe the clean-up of the environment is a national concern and one which must be addressed here in the House of Commons.

speakeroldname: Mr. Mel Gass (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although the disposal and destruction of hazardous wastes in Canada are the responsibility of the provinces, the federal Government is actively involved in the search for solutions. Not one government can confront this issue on its own. It is for this reason that the federal-provincial Canadian Council of Resource and Environment Ministers has initiated work on the development of a national action plan for the management of hazardous wastes in Canada. Along with this initiative, CCREM has already developed and implemented a national action plan aimed at eliminating PCBs from the Canadian environment. The plan has four basic objectives; first, the establishment of destruction facilities; second, the creation of national standards for the transportation and destruction of PCBs; third, the creation of national environmental quality objectives for PCBs; fourth, the dissemination of factual information on PCBs.

May 29, 1986
Adjournment Debate
Ever since the Kenora spill, PCBs have been of particular concern to the Canadian public. Hardly a day seems to pass when there is not a new revelation of PCBs found at yet another location. This is a concern which I believe will be alleviated by the initiatives now under way by the Canadian Council of Resource and Environment Ministers. It is a concern which will be further alleviated by the fact that technologies do exist to destroy PCBs.
On May 2, the Hon. Member for Welland (Mr. Pietz) questioned the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) about a hazardous waste disposal unit which will be tested at the Love Canal site this summer. I am happy to report that the unit in question was designed and built in Canada and was successfully tested for PCB destruction. This plasma arc destruction unit is mounted on a 45-foot trailer and can be readily moved to PCB disposal sites. The unit is but one of a number of fixed and transportable mobile PCB destruction technologies which are coming on line for commercial application in Canada.
On April 5 of this year, the Ontario Government gazetted a new regulation under its Environmental Protection Act for transportable mobile PCB destruction facilities. This effort to regulate these facilities is a major step forward in eliminating PCBs from the Canadian environment. With this new regulation, companies can now begin applying to the province for approval to operate their PCB destruction facilities.
Initiatives are now under way in other provinces in Canada to rid ourselves of PCB wastes. British Columbia has taken an active role in determining suitable transportable mobile technologies for destroying PCBs in western Canada. Alberta has selected a site for its hazardous waste facility and expects it to be fully operational by 1988. Saskatchewan has established a permanent indoor facility in Regina for a mobile low concentration PCB treatment process which has been in use in the province since 1983. Quebec has initiated a search for a suitable location for destruction facilities. These are just some of the initiatives now taking place across Canada.
As our world becomes more complex, so do the environmental problems we must confront. Special efforts to reach a consensus on the best solutions for different problems are required if solutions are to be found and acted upon. PCBs provide a model of federal-provincial co-operation in confronting a problem and finding solutions to that problem. The lessons learned on this issue will no doubt be of immense use to us in solving other issues which threaten our environment.
